name: Hair fibers
lead: Hair fibers, also called hair-building or concealing fibers, are small coloured strands, usually made from keratin or cotton, sold as a loose powder in a shaker or sprinkler. When shaken or dusted over thinning hair they cling to existing hairs and make them look thicker, which reduces the visible contrast between scalp and hair [2]. Well-known brands include Toppik, Nanogen and Viviscal's fibers, and a published laboratory study analysed all three [2].

The product is a camouflage, not a treatment. It does not change hair growth or follicle activity, and its effect lasts until the hair is washed. Dermatology literature lists topical hair fibers alongside wigs, extensions and scalp micropigmentation among the camouflage options clinicians discuss with people who have hair loss [3][4].

Published evidence is limited. A hospital-based laboratory and clinical study found similar camouflage effects across five brands in androgenetic alopecia, telogen effluvium and trichotillomania, with patients expressing satisfaction and no adverse effects reported, but the fibers did not adhere to bare patches in alopecia areata [2]. A cross-sectional study of patient satisfaction and adverse effects of fiber fillers also exists [5].

paras: Fibers differ by composition. The 2017 study analysed five organic products by scanning electron microscopy and X-ray microanalysis. Three, described as cotton-based or plant-derived keratin, appeared as parallel-arranged fibers rich in carbon, oxygen and silicon. The other two, one made from sheep's wool keratin (Toppik) and one described as positively charged keratin (Nanogen), resembled natural hair in shape and were rich in sulfur [2].

Fibers are sold in a range of shades intended to match natural hair colour, and are commonly paired with a hairspray-type fixing mist, which relates them to thickening sprays and hairline concealer powders as part of the same camouflage category.

The fibers are charged and bind to existing hair shafts, adding apparent thickness and covering gaps through which scalp is visible [2]. Because they need hair to grip, the study found they did not adhere to bare areas of alopecia areata, so the effect depends on residual hair [2]. In the wider context of pattern hair loss, Wikipedia lists styling the remaining hair to make loss less apparent as part of management [1], and camouflage reviews describe such measures as aiding confidence and reducing stigma without treating the underlying loss [3][4].

The most detailed published work is a 2017 study from a trichology unit in a tertiary hospital. It combined electron microscopy of five fiber brands with an in-vivo application test in patients. The authors reported that camouflage effects were similar across brands in androgenetic alopecia, telogen effluvium and trichotillomania; that patients were clearly satisfied; that no adverse effects were reported and that medical treatment did not need to change; that fibers did not stain clothing and were easily removed by washing or blow-drying; and that they were not helpful in alopecia areata. The authors suggested that fibers may reduce the psychological burden of alopecia. The number of patients was not stated in the article [2].

A cross-sectional study listed as examining patient satisfaction and adverse effects after topical hair fiber use also exists [5]. Reviews of hair camouflage, including one focused on Black women with alopecia, describe topical fibers, wigs and micropigmentation as widely used and affordable, and recommend tailoring choice to the patient while avoiding adhesives and high-tension styling that can worsen hair loss [3][4].
No randomized controlled trial of hair fibers is available.

In the studies above, no adverse effects were reported [2]. The 2017 study noted that the fibers did not stain clothing and washed out easily, and that they did not adhere to bare skin [2]. Camouflage reviews note that cosmetic procedures are intrinsically safe but that the surrounding styling practices, such as adhesives or tight braiding, can harm hair [3].

Hair fibers are a frequent topic in forums that discuss thinning hair. Archived r/tressless threads include community searches on the product category and personal questions about whether and when to tell a dating partner that fibers are in use, illustrating the concealment and disclosure concerns that come up around them [6][7].

timeline.event: Spanish hospital study compares five hair-fiber brands by electron microscopy and in patients [2].

lore.intro: Hair fibers are discussed as a fast, reversible cosmetic option for thinning hair, and threads also address how to handle disclosure to partners [6][7].

claims.claim: Fibers instantly hide thinning without treating it
claims.believers: Users describe them as a quick way to reduce scalp visibility at the part and hairline, and some discuss the social side of using them [6][7].
claims.experts: A clinical study found similar camouflage effects across brands in androgenetic alopecia, telogen effluvium and trichotillomania, with patient satisfaction and no adverse effects reported [2].

claims.claim: Fibers work anywhere on the scalp
claims.believers: Product marketing and some user discussion treat them as universal concealers.
claims.experts: The same study found they did not stick to bald areas in alopecia areata, so residual hair is required [2].

claims.claim: Using fibers will be noticed or can be hidden from partners
claims.believers: A thread asks how and when to tell girls the poster dates that they use fibers, reflecting concerns about detectability [6].
claims.experts: No published study has examined how often fibers are detected by observers.
